title: Build connected AI: Orchestrate tools and agents with registries and ADK
description: Scale is the new challenge for enterprise agent teams: not building agents, but governing hundreds of them. This Cloud Next session covers Agent Registry as the single source of truth for agents and MCP servers, SpecBoost for automatically generating and enriching API specs from logs, Agent Identity with SPIFFE-based per-agent credentials, and a Klook (APAC travel platform) case study showing how they used this stack to build a supply research multi-agent system.

segments.heading: The challenge has shifted: from building agents to governing hundreds
segments.text: Last year at Cloud Next, the challenge was building agents that connect to data sources. A2A was just announced. MCP was new and exciting. The challenge has now shifted: organizations have hundreds of agents that often duplicate work, dozens of MCP servers doing the same thing because teams were each building their own, and no governance layer. Three specific pain points: (1) discoverability: builders cannot find what agents or MCP servers already exist in their organization; (2) building on top: even when they find something, integrating securely is non-trivial; (3) governance: platform teams cannot ensure that only authorized agents call the right set of tools.

segments.heading: Agent Registry: single source of truth for agents, MCPs, and models
segments.text: Agent Registry is the central catalog for all agents, MCP servers, and registered models in a Google Cloud project. It supports registering third-party MCP servers if no existing entry is found. Available via portal UI, API, and SDK. ADK has built-in primitives to discover and call registered agents and MCP servers using just a few lines of code by providing the registry ID. The portal shows: registered agents with their skills and A2A agent card details, registered MCP servers with tool lists and usage metrics, and generated code snippets for ADK integration.

segments.heading: Agent Identity: SPIFFE-based per-agent credentials and secure vault
segments.text: Agent Identity is a SPIFFE-based identity standard that gives each deployed agent its own unique identity (a SPIFFE ID). The identity lifecycle matches the agent lifecycle: created at deployment, revoked when the agent is deleted. This removes the previous pattern where a shared service account was used by all agents in a project, making granular permission management impossible. Agent Identity also includes a Secure Credentials Vault for storing API keys and OAuth credentials per agent, so developers do not need to manage secret sprawl themselves. OAuth configurations (two-legged for service-to-service, three-legged for user-delegated access) are stored in the vault and associated with the specific agent identity.

segments.heading: SpecBoost: from no API specs to enriched, agent-ready MCP servers
segments.text: Enterprise APIs commonly lack rich, accurate OpenAPI specifications. Agents calling underspecified APIs hallucinate parameter names, call endpoints incorrectly, or fail silently. SpecBoost (enabled in API Hub) solves this with three modes: (1) generate: produce API specs from scratch by analyzing API gateway logs (Apigee runtime or Cloud Storage log buckets); (2) boost: take existing specs and enrich them so they are more agent-readable (better descriptions, error examples, parameter semantics); (3) merge: compare generated specs against documentation to detect drift when engineers deploy API changes without updating docs. No spec is published without human sign-off. Vision: API documentation becomes automatically live-updated whenever an API changes. One-click conversion from enriched spec in API Hub to a registered MCP service in Agent Registry is in progress.

segments.heading: Klook case study: supply research multi-agent system
segments.text: Klook is the largest online experiences platform in APAC with 300,000 products across 4,000 destinations and 65 million experiences booked in 2025. The supply research process was manual, slow, and unable to cover the long tail of opportunities. Agents miss seasonal windows (cherry blossom tours, Christmas markets) if insights are delayed by days of manual research. Klook built a multi-agent supply research system: an orchestrator agent coordinates multiple specialized sub-agents, each analyzing a different social platform (one per platform, running in parallel). Key ADK decision: use standalone sub-agents rather than skills for sub-tasks that need their own context and parallel execution. ADK enabled fast wiring. Three learnings: (1) speed: ADK makes new agents fast to build and wire together; (2) reusability: all agents go into Agent Registry so they are discovered by other teams (for example, the YouTube analysis agent also supports voice-of-customer use cases); (3) continuous optimization: non-technical domain experts access published agents via Gemini Enterprise and provide direct feedback. An in-house supply quality agent then evaluates Klook's own catalog against market needs using internal booking data. All internal APIs are being progressively converted to MCP servers and centralized in Agent Registry for governance. Result: workflows that took days now complete in hours.

title: AI tools for human creativity
description: An inside look at Google's latest creative tools from the people using them to make film, art, games, music and more. See how musicians, designers, coders, and filmmakers at Google Creative Lab and Labs are using Google Flow, Antigravity, Genie and Google Flow Music in their creative processes.
entities: Around the World in Good News

segments.heading: Creative Lab's job, and the one thing that is not changing
segments.text:
Matthew Carey and Alex Chen open the first ever builder stage at Google I/O. Both are from Google Creative Lab, a team of writers, designers, coders and filmmakers that collaborates with research and product teams across Google, plays with the latest AI models, and explores the edges of what is possible.

Both came to the work through music. Alex grew up playing viola and piano and making music, and got into coding early, so his whole life has been an attempt to blend code, design and music. Matthew was a choir boy, then a theater kid, then got into making films, then copywriting, then interactive art, which is when he first met Creative Lab. They describe themselves as creatively omnivorous: they love to make things, and now they love helping shape the tools that help other people make things.

The framing they offer is that technology is a blank canvas, and it is human imagination that shapes technology into new stories and new ways of telling stories. They acknowledge the pace directly: if it feels like things are moving fast, they feel it too from inside Google, where a new tool or model appears every day that you are supposed to stay on top of.

The counterweight is their central claim. Some things are not changing at all. Human collaboration has always been at the center of the creative process and has to stay there. That is why they value sessions where people can talk to each other about what they are using, what is working, what they like and dislike, share work and inspire each other.

A Creative Lab collaborator had spoken in the previous day's keynote about Google building tools with creatives and for creatives, working with artists outside Google to shape the technology. This session is the inside view: creatives working within Google, going deep on Google Flow, Flow Music, Antigravity, AI Studio, and building interactive worlds with Project Genie.

The format is deliberate. The speakers were asked not just to show what they made but to go deep on how they made it: sketches, and how much work and love went in. Matthew adds that his favorite part is the why.

segments.heading: Sanchit Sawaria: which software did you use is the wrong question
segments.text:
Sanchit Sawaria is a design generalist working on Google Flow, making images, videos and products. He was central to conceiving, designing and launching Google Flow a year earlier, and has since been embedded in the Google Labs design and UX team on Flow, helping evolve it into a full AI creative studio. He frames his talk as a conversation between the student version of himself and the professional version, both using the tools in front of them.

In design school he was in awe of the work around him, and his favorite question to ask his superiors was which software they used to make something. He never got a straight answer. The most common response was that this was the wrong question, and the question he should be asking was what the thought process was.

His point is that nothing has changed. The current version of the wrong question is what was your prompt. What is wrong with both questions is the assumption they carry: that access to the prompt, or access to the same tools, is enough to replicate someone's ideas and process. It is not, because it is not about the tools, it is about the fundamentals.

He considers himself fortunate to have gone to a design school that taught no design tools at all. The foundational program focused on design drawing and analytical drawing. They painted color wheels with paintbrushes and drew type with pencils, and worked through foundational courses in gestalt, composition and typography. That preparation meant he never had to rely on a tool and could use whichever tool he wanted.

The trajectory he describes is additive rather than replacing. He started with the pencil and the brush. On graduating he used the digital versions of those tools, and picked up 3D modeling and motion design, which he could do because the fundamentals were strong. Now what he uses with AI tools is his vocabulary. He stresses that he has not left the pencil and the digital tools behind; he uses a mixture of all of them.

segments.heading: Prompts as design vocabulary, with three worked examples
segments.text:
Sanchit explains why vocabulary is the operative asset. He had to go through using manual tools in order to learn the terminology, and now he can use those terms in his prompts.

On what it means to be a good prompter, he does not think there is one good way. For him, prompts are informed by the fundamentals learned in design school, internalized and then showing up in the writing. His prompts never follow the same structure, but he makes sure to talk about texture, color and composition, and if there is type in the image, he defines what kind of type.

The first example uses a ray traced 3D rendered style, so his experience with 3D modeling and rendering pays off in referencing the right terminology. He invites the audience to imagine what the prompt would produce, then shows it. The specific lever is Art Nouveau typography: because he knows what Art Nouveau typography looks like, he can create it with precision and knows in advance how it will look. He draws the distinction sharply. There is an enormous difference between saying elegant typography and saying elegant Art Nouveau typography. That is the difference between having gone through a design curriculum, and being an actual type designer, versus someone who is only referencing things.

The second example is precise about hex codes. He created the color palette separately, made sure it was the exact color he wanted, and included the hex values in the prompt. The prompt has a composition section, then a photography section specifying a 300 millimeter lens, chosen because he wants less distortion.

The third example sets color and decides on a subject, and its last line is the one he calls really important: off center, rule of thirds, section composition. Had he not gone through the composition course in design school, he would not have been able to communicate and articulate the idea properly.

His conclusion is that everyone can have good ideas, but you need to be able to articulate them, and that ability comes from experience.

segments.heading: Process and iteration are what make the work ownable
segments.text:
The other thing that has not changed for Sanchit is that he had a process before and still has one, and the process is what makes work ownable.

He notes that a lot of people talk about one shotting things, and while it is amazing that this is possible, it is not satisfying for him. The only way he can author work is through iteration. Even when a prompt looks perfect and reusable, he may have gone through many iterations of that prompt to craft it and get the language right.

He used to start with sketches and still starts with sketches, because sometimes that is the easiest way to get thoughts onto paper. He shows two examples side by side: on the left a 3D model he made and rendered into an animation with ray tracing software, and on the right sketches used to visualize a furniture line, then rendered with Nano Banana inside Google Flow.

Going deeper into that process, Flow has both image making and video making tools. In the image editor he starts with the sketch of a chair, then changes the legs, changes the background, adds a polar bear, and arrives at a composition. The detail he calls out is that he did not think of the cats at the beginning; they showed up somehow. That is what he means by a process: you discover the work through multiple iterations. The image editor records version history on the right, which is what he loves about working in it.

On character work, he used to have to learn to rig a character, which he did not enjoy. Now he can explore a character's movement logic directly in Flow with frame animation. He is careful not to overclaim: character rigging is not dead, and it is still the best way to get real control over a character. But for a graphic designer entering the world of characters and 3D modeling, this is a good entry point.

His example is a character built in the character creator tool in Flow, called Rothko, which is an empty vessel whose beverage changes with the day: a cocktail on vacation, a soft serve on a hot summer day. After making the still images, he can produce many variations of one character, then explore motion dynamics and things that cannot be rigged, such as liquid simulation. He shows melancholic Rothko, surprised Rothko, and a third that is probably listening to music.

On iteration volume, he used to iterate and now iterates a lot more. What AI provides is abundance, which he calls both a blessing and a curse: you can have an infinite number of variations of one thing, but you then have to know where to stop and declare one of them the one. His answer is organization inside Flow. He is making little tweaks with every variation, so even with hundreds of variations of the same character, the fiftieth might be the one selected, and it is valuable to be able to see the journey of how one thing was crafted.

He states his position on craft plainly. Working on something for a long time and spending time on it is what craft is about. It is not just about using your hands, and craft is not dead.

segments.heading: Making things that make things: custom tools inside Flow
segments.text:
Sanchit's next line marks a shift in what a designer's output is. He used to make things; now he makes things that make things. He is a graphic designer who now makes products, and the way he can make products is through coding in Flow.

Inside Flow he can create his own tool, as he could in another surface such as AI Studio, but with an important advantage: he has access to all his assets, which already exist in his Flow projects, so he can build tools and use the same assets.

His example is a style he developed over ten years. He used to love working with gradients, and he built a pulsating continuous gradient animation by making vector shapes, animating them, and exploring blending modes between those shapes. What he then did was distil that style into a brush, and he says it felt like inventing a new medium.

He could own the result because there is a direct connection between the two images, but the new one is interactive. It genuinely felt like using a brush he had never played with before, with parameters adjustable in real time: he could change the parameters on the fly, change the gradient colors, and change the animation speed. The reason he could do it at all is that he had already been working with gradients in previous versions of the tools.

segments.heading: The Primordial Soup identity, and why isolation costs you objectivity
segments.text:
Sanchit used to make logotypes as a type designer; now he makes animated logotypes.

The project he shares is an identity design for Darren Aronofsky's AI studio, Primordial Soup. He wanted something that reads as microscopic life while also being lettering and typography. He started with a rough sketch, took it to vector form, drew bezier curves, refined it heavily, then took it into Flow to render.

That rendering step is where the process changes, and he is direct that he could not have done it this easily before. He tried a subtle ink rendering with highlights, then explored more organic renderings. This is what he means by process: he could have stopped at the black and white vector, but he wants to introduce more steps, and AI lets him. Finally he took frames from the organic renderings done in Flow, took the first frame, and animated the logotype.

His framing of the payoff inverts the usual efficiency argument. He is not trying to make his work faster. You can, but that is not his aim. He is trying to make the process richer, sometimes by introducing more steps in between, and he is obsessed with pushing the medium forward.

The last and most important part of his process is that he works with people, and always did. He shows a hazy photograph of himself and a roommate looking at offset print proofs at night, alongside a photo of Reed, a friend from the Flow team he still collaborates with.

Critique and collaboration are essential to his work, because without them he loses all objectivity. He cannot work in isolation, so discussing ideas with other people and getting their feedback simply makes the work better.

He closes on the specific risk this technology introduces. With AI it is very easy to isolate yourself and make your own tools, where everything is bespoke and tuned to your liking. But we make work for others, so it is important that the conversation keeps going.

segments.heading: Khyati Trehan: vibe coding as a way to broaden what a designer can do
segments.text:
Kaloyan Kolev and Khyati Trehan come up together. Matthew introduces them as two prolific vibe coders who go deep on everything from AI Studio to Antigravity to the new custom tools in Flow, and notes what he values most: they are generous, always sharing what they made and the thinking behind it in team chats. Khyati's work reminds him that taste and craft have always mattered and always will, regardless of tools. Kaloyan's work feels to him like a first hand look at a new kind of creative coder, moving fluidly between hardware, filmmaking and other mediums.

Kaloyan introduces himself as a creative technologist who uses code every day. Khyati introduces herself as a graphic designer who does not write code at all. Both have found value in the practice of coding.

They define the term for the room. Vibe coding is describing what you want in plain language and using an LLM (a large language model, the kind of model that generates text and code) to write code that does it. They have been prolific vibe coders for about a year, and it has dramatically transformed their creative process.

Khyati's background is deliberately varied: designer and visual artist, a long stretch as a type design intern, an AR phase, many editorial illustrations for newspapers. She describes it as a lot of bouncing around, and says she has always tried to broaden those labels and ask what else she is capable of, and what learning a new skill unlocks.

Her method for learning something new is to start with something old, because it makes the unlock obvious: you literally have a before and after in front of you. Her example pairs stage visuals she made for Lollapalooza in 2023 with a more recent interactive sketch that borrows elements from them and reinvents them.

She describes the experience as being back in design school: making things, learning about libraries, asking questions, figuring out how to use sound. Those sketches turned into a personal assignment where she takes favorite quotes from books she is reading and turns them into expressive typography posters, but only when vibe coding or interaction could help convey the meaning better. Her favorite of the three reads: it is a simple idea, but also stupid, and the thing is, when stupid ideas work, they become genius ideas.

segments.heading: Shipping the tool alongside the artifact, and designing from inside the room
segments.text:
Khyati identifies a change in what she publishes. Now that she is making both the final asset and the tool that helped her get there, she shares both.

What is wonderful about that is a small button in the corner: other people can not only play with the tool, they can riff on it. She admits this was culturally new for her in design terms. She expected to feel cagey, because it is like sharing your Photoshop file or your Cinema 4D file, essentially your working file. Instead it was surprisingly gratifying to see someone take it further and make it their own. She had built it for one purpose; they made it more broadly useful for themselves.

Her explanation for why so many new ideas, micro-interactions and features are emerging is that she now gets to be both the designer and the user at the same time.

Working in AI Studio also gives her access to an ecosystem of Google models and APIs, so she can work with Translate, with sound, with Lyria (Google's generative music model), with text to speech, and with Maps. She built Around the World in Good News to set the tone for 2026 with something positive. It helps you explore uplifting historical events and stories of human achievement from across the globe and across time, and it is grounded in Google Search, so there are buttons that take you to an actual article.

She took the ecosystem much further with Machine Telephone, which is the telephone game played between you and Google's APIs and models. You enter an input and pass it sequentially through whichever medium or model you pick, and you watch how context shifts, gets translated, and sometimes gets misunderstood along the chain. Her input was marine diatom. She asked Gemini to write a poem about it, then asked what location on the map Gemini would pick if inspired by that poem, then turned that location into a song, that song into a color palette, that palette into a material, and onward.

She had wanted to make a game like this for a long time: a telephone game between unlikely participants. The origin was advice that you should look for inspiration outside your field, because it is in those strange middles that you usually find new ideas.

She took her time on it, marinating on details that do not usually get the love they deserve. She names the assumption she is pushing against: that with AI you hit a button and something magically pops up. Sometimes that does happen, but even when she gets something in one shot she makes sure not to stop there, because good ideas take time. Had she not slept on it, she might not have thought of the tiny dog ear in the corner of the input card that signals you have pressed Enter there.

Her description of how the process itself feels different is the most quotable line in her section. It is like the difference between seeing a blueprint of a room and also getting to be in it. You can gauge the space, and maybe design better for it.

The consequence is a change in nerve. Where she would otherwise have resorted to standard UI, which is helpful when designing for millions of users, in these cases she feels much braver about departing from convention and reaching for delight and identity. Her example is loading states, which should be boring and are not.

Her conclusion, as she vibe codes her way through building tools, is that it is becoming even clearer that her years of practice, skill, knowledge, expertise and experience still pay off.

segments.heading: Kaloyan Kolev: speed, control and improvisation
segments.text:
Kaloyan's background is in video and music production, with computer graphics studied in college. Today his whole practice is building creative tools and generative art with high tech software and low tech hardware.

Thinking about tools as both a user and a builder, he names three values he looks for:

Speed. He wants to move from idea to result as fast as possible, and equally wants to move on from an idea without feeling guilty about time wasted.

Control. He wants to be hands on in every part of the process, and to move between very high level and very specific very quickly.

Improvisation. Coming from music, he wants everything to feel like a guitar pedal: surfaces and systems set up in a way that allows for happy accidents and free flowing exploration.

His read on what changed is precise about the trade-off. Code as a medium always gave a lot of control, but at the sacrifice of speed and improvisation. A year earlier, building your own tools was often more trouble than it was worth. AI tools have now reached the point where much of the overhead is gone: you do not need to get hung up on syntax and debugging, you can explore an unfamiliar library, and it feels casual, quick and spontaneous.

His illustration of how far this goes is a change in habit. He used to write ideas down in his notes app. Now he opens AI Studio on his phone, writes the idea there, fires off the prompt and moves on, and when he comes back there is a first version of the app waiting for him. Ideas feel lightweight and quick that way.

His practice with code has become almost improvisational. Working with designers on commercial projects or brainstorming visuals for himself, he now often starts directly in code and builds a web app.

The team example is Project Genie. The designers had to work out how to create an interface around a brand new category, a world model, which is neither a video nor an image but a whole world. The designers came up with a volumetric 3D sphere effect, which the team built out in code along with custom sliders so they could dial in exactly what was needed. That worked well because everything was made in code and could be handed off to front end engineers, and both sides spoke the same language.

segments.heading: Building tools around a medium: Super Looper, ASCII Film Studio, Flow tools
segments.text:
Kaloyan's next method is to take his favorite parts of his favorite software and build around them. He loves playing with image editing tools and spamming contrast, blur and sharpness in a loop, so he built a tool that does exactly that. He calls it Super Looper: you chain blur, sharpen, blur, sharpen, press Enter, and run it a hundred times in a row, watching patterns emerge from the way the algorithms are set up.

Sometimes the medium comes before the tool. When Gemini 3 came out, he discovered it was very good at making animated ASCII drawings in p5.js (a JavaScript library for creative coding). He would ask for a short film, write the music himself, and the model would make the visuals, and he found them charming enough to build a tool around. He calls it ASCII Film Studio: you write your own short script on the left, tweak the settings, and Gemini makes the film.

He describes this as a new kind of co-creation between himself and the models, entirely through code, which is why he is excited about Flow tools, launched the previous day. Flow tools is a new coding layer inside Flow, and he hopes it lets many more creatives build tools like this inside Flow, using their own footage.

He worked on several tools for the starter gallery. His favorite is weirdcore, a box of ten trippy, glitchy visual effects that can be stacked and chained. What he loves most about it is the random button: you keep clicking it, get new combinations, and it feels spontaneous and improvisational, surfacing values you might not have considered if you were manually tweaking sliders.

segments.heading: Prototyping a dithering algorithm on real hardware, with an agent over SSH
segments.text:
Kaloyan also works a lot with hardware, and names the thing he has always hated about it: everything takes so long, because when you code something you have to run it on the actual device.

His project of the last three or four years is called reframe, an experimental camera using a color e-paper display, almost like a digital Polaroid. You take a picture and it stays on the screen even after the camera is turned off, but you can only have one photo at a time.

The technical constraint is what makes the project interesting. E-paper displays have a limited color palette, so every image has to be dithered before it goes on the display. Dithering is the technique of approximating colors the display cannot show by arranging the colors it can show in a pattern. Developing dithering algorithms is fun but normally slow, because you need to see the result on the actual screen.

He shows an unstaged photo from his kitchen, which he admits is embarrassingly messy, where he was prototyping a new dithering algorithm the previous week in Antigravity, another of Google's coding surfaces. The workflow he describes is the point: his agent was SSH'd into the camera (SSH being the standard protocol for opening a remote shell on another machine), it would prototype the algorithm, put it directly on the camera, he would look at the screen, give feedback, and iterate quickly, directly on the hardware.

On who these tools are for, he makes the case for a deliberately tiny audience. The audience for your own micro-tools can be just you, or you and your friends, loved ones or colleagues, so you can make them as weird and as specific as you want. If you want a crazy liquid chrome SVG border around every part of the UI, it is your tool, so go ahead. If you want to work with your own data, your own archives, or your community's archives, you can.

What he hopes the newfound accessibility of coding brings is an explosion of new projects, particularly interfaces built on top of archives: search engines, art projects and curatorial projects that can finally dig into digital archives which previously required a lot of code and a heavy coding background.

segments.heading: The provocation: speed comes with responsibility
segments.text:
Kaloyan ends with a deliberate provocation: he thinks it is possible to go too far with this.

The newfound ability to write and deploy code so fast comes with a responsibility. We should not be putting slop into the world, or making things for the sake of making, just to feel creative. Using a model to write the code does not mean we should stop paying attention to every detail, especially when sharing work with other people, with loved ones, with coworkers. His closing standard is that we should be respectful of our time, of our craft, and of our taste.

Matthew picks up the thread on personal software. He feels a genuine inflection point, and the thing that makes it interesting is that what he wants to make is entirely different from what someone else wants to make. He calls the silver chrome borders shallow, and that is the point: every person in the room would make something entirely different and unique to them. That is what the new Google Flow tools are for.

segments.heading: Kendall Rankin: a retreat playlist and a bespoke ambient filter in Flow Music
segments.text:
Matthew introduces Kendall Rankin and Henry Ives from the Flow Music team, a small team of thirteen people and a new member of Google's family of creative tools. He notes what he loves about their approach: music does not have to be one thing, it can be unique for everybody, and they use their own product for genuinely personal things in their own lives that are totally different from each other.

Kendall has had music at the core of her life since she was young, growing up in the gospel choir at church, and is passionate about music as a force for expression in everyday life and with the people we love. She was an engineer in undergrad, studying a technical field while keeping a passion for the creative world, then found Fusion, which is now Google Flow Music, and has been doing community and artist engagement work.

Henry is a percussionist and composer who does everything from film music to experimental improvisation to drumming in the 49ers drumline. A little over a year earlier he joined the team that would become Flow Music, out of interest in how the next generation of technology would shape the next era of music.

They level set before demonstrating anything. This could have been a product talk about new features, but what matters to them is that the tool allows experimentation, iteration and the creation of new music. The use cases they see broaden who becomes a creator and a musician, while also letting artists and professional musicians go deeper with the tooling.

Kendall's example comes from outside work. She hosts retreats for friends, family and people in her community, and believes community and connection are core to the human experience and to how we engage with music. Her question is how to use technology to enrich experiences that already connect us.

At the last retreat, the meditation session was especially popular: a moment to sit, look out at the Calistoga hills, and enjoy the time together. So she decided to create a playlist for the retreat. She thought about what feelings and emotions she wanted to evoke in the group, and tapped into a shared love of neo soul music that the group had discovered over dinner the night before.

In Flow Music she worked with the producer agent to craft a prompt communicating all of that: a five song playlist that evokes serenity and stillness and feels rich, moving and grounding. From that prompt she got five songs that she believes fit the bill.

She then took it a step further using spaces, which is Flow Music's version of music coded apps. She wanted a space that adds an ambient filter, atmospheric tones and shimmering effects to enrich the music she had already created. She came to the producer agent with that idea, asking it to create the audio filter and add the ethereal effects. It returned a first draft and allowed her to iterate.

The detail she flags as valuable is that the agent also broke down what it was doing and used the moment as a teaching opportunity, which mattered to someone who had a clear vision and the music but did not necessarily know how she would get there. From there they iterated back and forth to build the space.

In the demo, sliding the atmospheric filter to the right increases the atmospheric sounds so the track becomes hazier, and she then brings it down to highlight the shimmering effects. Any combination of the two effects works, and additional filters can be mixed in. What made it powerful for her was being able to add elements to both the tool and the music.

segments.heading: Henry Ives: prompting past genre to build a practice accompaniment
segments.text:
Henry notes that when he was putting his slides together, the Creative Lab team suggested it would be more personal to use a real picture of himself rather than a product photo, which he takes as a compliment to his photographer friend Cat. The picture is of his hands.

As a percussionist he has spent countless hours building fundamentals, and he has noticed that the way you spend those hours over the years shapes the type of player you become. Given a generative music creation platform, the question becomes how to make a practice routine a reflection of yourself. Generative music creates a genuinely new use case: you can create accompaniments to practice with that fit both the technical requirements of your exercise and steer you in the musical direction you want to go.

He set out to explore this with his favorite drum exercise, triplet rolls, and the sequence of failures is the useful part.

He started with a simple prompt: synthwave, steady kick drum pulse, 160 BPM, which is the tempo of the exercise. The Lyria model got the tempo right, but the vibe was too 1980s movie and too dramatic, not aesthetically what he wanted.

He moved to breakcore, a genre he loves for being energetic and exciting, and got more specific about the groove. This is a triplet exercise, so he needed a triplet groove, and Lyria took an interesting interpretation of that. But he realized the genre does not lend itself well to the exercise.

He kept bouncing between genres. Swing always had the rhythmic style he needed, but aesthetically it came out very romantic montage and very coffee shop, also not what he wanted. He went back to electronic music wanting more energy and tried drum and bass, similar to breakcore, but this is not a genre where the triplet groove he needs is commonly heard. He notes this is actually an active area of research: how to make Lyria cleverly reconcile prompts that are somewhat conflicting or require some creativity.

The realization that resolved it is the transferable lesson. If he is prompting at the level of genre, the results are going to be generic, basically by definition. That forced him to think about what he actually wanted to hear and which skills he wanted to train. For percussionists, rolls are supposed to be smooth and connected while staying in great time. Thinking about that got him to a prompt specifying a particular synth sound, a specific type of beat, and even a specific snare material. The result was far more him.

segments.heading: Building bespoke instruments: a vocal chopper and a granular synth
segments.text:
Henry is also a music composer, and has noticed over the years that the more of your identity you put into the process, the more expressive the final piece will be. That raises the same question in a different place: how do you build a process that is a reflection of you.

One answer he found even before AI is to either collect or create unique tools. As you accrue a bespoke tool belt, the process becomes more your own and the pieces become more unique.

His current interest is chopping up vocals, specifically pitched up gospel sounds, which is what he has been listening to. He went to Flow Music and to spaces and iterated until he found a gospel track worth sampling. Then he spent time thinking about the aesthetics and the functionality that could turn that song into a playable instrument. The demo plays a phrase built around the line "when we sing together".

He is candid about the presentation. He is not sure it comes across well as a final piece, but he had a lot of fun, staying up too late while working on the presentation and getting distracted trying to play it. He also admits to some movie magic: he recorded it at half time and sped it up. He thinks he can play it in real time and offers to demonstrate at the demo booth afterward.

The second niche process is granular synthesis, which he explains simply: you take an existing track, chop it into tiny grains, and make a new ambient textured sustain out of them. He went to Flow Music and thought through which aesthetics and which functionality would make a version of a granular synth that felt like what he wanted to express.

segments.heading: Sharing spaces, and the human at the center
segments.text:
Kendall closes the music section on the two directions the team cares about: broadening who has access, and deepening for people who already have craft. Henry showed tools that deepen for artists and producers, so she shows a mini keyboard the team created. As a vocalist who does not play instruments, she has found it genuinely fun to use the instruments you can build with spaces, both to develop an understanding of how these things work and to create new sounds she can sing on top of.

Having spent the talk on making things more unique, more personal and more bespoke, she names the counterweight. Art and music are about sharing, cross-pollination of ideas, and the social aspect. Their simple mechanism for that is letting you share spaces with others.

Her example is Colby, whom she describes as an evil wizard on the Flow Music team and a fantastic music producer. When spaces first launched he was tasked with exploring it and making a lot of spaces, and he shared all of them with the team. Her favorite is an effect randomizer knob, where he took a set of curated effects and exposed them all through one big knob. She was also up too late finalizing the presentation, throwing old demos into it and finding delightfully unexpected combinations of sounds and effects.

The conclusion she draws across all of the presentations is that the human is truly at the center of how this technology is used to create, whether the goal is broadening or deepening.

segments.heading: Shashwath Santosh and Samuel Lawton: from generative images to explorable worlds
segments.text:
Matthew introduces the final pair. Most creatives get into this work because they have hungry, novelty seeking minds, and as models get more capable he believes ravenous curiosity is an innately human quality that cannot be replaced. Shashwath Santosh and Samuel Lawton are multidisciplinary creatives who have been spelunking into the frontier of world models: designers, tinkerers and builders, but really creative explorers. They build worlds, imagine worlds, jump into them, work out how to operate inside them, then share what they learn, constantly sending back what look like surreal vacation videos from the places they visit in Genie.

They have been creative partners at Google for essentially the entirety of this AI era, and in that time have played with, studied and stretched the boundaries of many AI tools, most recently Project Genie.

They lay out the progression compactly. Just over three years earlier, the state of the art was generative imagery: type a few words, get an image back. That graduated to video. A few months before this talk, it became possible to generate entire worlds, worlds that can be explored and interacted with in real time.

The simplest way to create a world is with text prompts. Ask to be a surfer riding a wave and you get something back where the physics of a video model combine with game like controls: you decide the direction you move in, and the environment expands to adapt.

As they prompted more with words, they began testing wordplay, including an attempt to create a portal between two contrasting worlds. The interactivity made these good mediums for visualizing complex scenes and thought experiments, including stepping into Plato's cave.

The most evident novelty, though, was navigating the world as a character. It completely changed how they experienced the world, and they consider it what set the model apart from the rest of the industry.

segments.heading: Testing what a character can do by isolating variables
segments.text:
The question that followed from character navigation was whether, if Genie could create infinite environments, the characters could do infinite things.

To understand the right prompting etiquette for characters, they ran quick tests that isolated single variables. They made the environment a big white lab containing one giant ladder, so they could test whether the model knew how to make a character climb, and how well it understood a simple concept like jump. They moved on to more nuanced actions: interacting with furniture, using electronic devices. All of these tests told them what the model could and could not do.

The cognitive leap from words to worlds was large enough that there was often considerable dissonance between the world you imagined in your head and the one you actually received.

segments.heading: Nano Banana as a visual steering engine, and the origin of world remixing
segments.text:
The dissonance problem was resolved by a different model. Nano Banana arrived, and they suddenly had a very strong image model available.

Because they are visual creatives and this is a visual model, they realized they could steer Genie through imagery, using Nano Banana as a visual engine to bias the model toward a specific visual style, whether photorealistic or stylized.

The other major capability Nano Banana unlocked was remixability. They could iterate on an existing world, locking in a specific environment while experimenting with different characters. They noticed that Genie had underlying knowledge of physics and the natural world, which affected body mechanics and the level of control across a variety of characters.

This granular experimentation honed their intuition for what the model could do, and it sparked the foundational idea of world remixing, which is now a feature in the product. It lets you fork a specific world, much as you would fork a code base, and perform transformative world edits: style, environment, character and more.

segments.heading: Exploiting visual biases: motion blur for speed, a sketched racetrack
segments.text:
With the visual steering path established, they leaned into the visual biases they found in the model.

If you wanted a car in a world to go faster, all you had to do was add motion blur to the source image, and Genie would do the heavy lifting, propelling the car into motion with much more speed and acceleration than before.

The same held for a skydiving example. Take the image, change it to winter, add some floating rings, and you have a much richer and more engaging experience complete with objectives and game mechanics, all from a handful of image edits.

Nano Banana also let them implement game mechanics by sketching exactly where elements should go. Starting from a photo of a backyard, Samuel sketched how he wanted a racetrack to run around a tree. With simple prompts he increased the fidelity and defined his character, and in Genie he was then driving that exact track with the right curves, in the same backyard.

segments.heading: Every photo in the camera roll as a game cartridge
segments.text:
At this point they recognized the creative potential hidden in the casual photos everyone captures every day. With Genie it was as if every photo in the camera roll was suddenly a game cartridge.

One example was taken at the Natural History Museum. Samuel had always wanted to step into the dioramas, and now they could explore one as the water buffalo. What he points out is that Genie expands on the details in the source image to create a fully interactive environment, using its world knowledge. Another example was a toy car, which they took drifting around the office.

A teammate, Arden, had the idea of making his own toys. He tested whether he could get Genie to activate his pipe cleaner worm, and it did. The unlock was that the worm could interact with marbles placed around it. Where they had previously used Nano Banana to add game mechanics, they now realized they could do the same thing by physically arranging artifacts in the real world, photographing them, and letting the model work out how to handle it.

Arden then tried a pipe cleaner human, and it worked exactly as imagined, entirely bypassing any complex 3D rigging setup. All it took was a simple image and text prompts. Before long the figure was scoring goals and riding a bicycle, and by placing the character on a bicycle, Genie arrived at the most natural way to combine the props and let the same character move differently.

They tried photos of themselves too. Samuel shows himself on a boat, where he can now paddle and look around, and notes they could go a step further and use Nano Banana to alter the style of the image being stepped into.

They also noticed the experience of Genie felt drastically different moving from standard monitors to bigger screens. That led to a question about perspective: humans are very familiar with their own experiences and points of view, so what about perspectives we are not familiar with and could never experience otherwise.

The team began experimenting with photos of their pets, to see familiar environments through their points of view, and this is where Genie's photorealism and biomechanics stood out. A cat navigates the apartment gracefully, whips its tail playfully in the air, and climbs over furniture without missing a step. A gecko expertly scales the walls of its surroundings, creating a vantage point you would otherwise never see. A hamster waddles around a table, whimsically interacting with the toys in its environment, and Genie sneaks in a double jump, which Shashwath finds consistently funny. Every animal shown belongs to their teammate Jocelyn.

They then used New York City as a test ground. From a photo of an iconic yellow cab, they could drive it around on their phones, and Genie intelligently adapted its character logic to the physical attributes of the object: a truck moves differently from the taxi, feeling more top heavy, and Samuel's feet naturally start pedaling as he begins moving on a bicycle.

Genie felt entirely different again on mobile, which they found to be the perfect platform to run around, capture and play. They tested that hypothesis with early prototypes, and the sandbox version was available to try at the event.

segments.heading: Street View inside Project Genie
segments.text:
The limitation in the real world examples is that Genie is given only a limited view of its surroundings, so some environments are not reflected as a one to one representation of reality.

The feature that addresses this launched the previous day: by leveraging existing Google tools and data, researchers implemented Street View as a native feature within Project Genie.

Using Street View, Samuel can scan around an environment, select a frame, and lock in a character: in this case a spaceship flying over the Golden Gate Bridge, or a bald eagle soaring over El Capitan. The capability, stated plainly, is that you can transport yourself anywhere in the world and explore that real world environment as any character you can imagine.

segments.heading: What else could the model do: creatives as the ones who find the edges
segments.text:
The defining through line of their time at Google, and of every experiment shown, was an attempt to answer one question: what else could the model do.

Their argument for why this is the creative's job is the closing thesis of the session. In a time of abundant research, it is up to creatives to discover the edges of the model, and thereby the use cases that matter. These things do not come with user manuals; they come with inventive play and creative critical discourse. Creatives get to write those manuals, and in doing so they begin to see the world differently.

The consequence is that everything around you becomes a potential playable character, and you start imagining interactions that do not exist. Shashwath uses the concrete spheres that are everywhere on the event grounds as an example: he had always wanted to take one for a spin, and shows how he did it.

He adds that they sometimes test things in places they probably should not, including during a section of the previous day's keynote, and, live on stage, controlling a butterfly flying around the room they are all sitting in.

His closing line reframes the whole session as an invitation rather than a demonstration. In a time when these worlds can be infinite, this is how they use Genie, and the question is how you would.

title: Cursor 101 part 2
description:
In this workshop, we introduce Cursor for newcomers , the surfaces, agent modes, models, and rules and skills that make you productive in a real codebase.

Key topics covered:

Surfaces:

Work in a familiar IDE view, an agent-first Agent Window, or the CLI. Cloud agents, the iOS app, and automations extend the same workflow beyond your laptop.

Agent modes:

Use Ask to explore a codebase read-only, Plan to design a change without editing, Debug to focus on fixing behavior, and Multitask to run independent agents in parallel.

Understand any codebase:

Point an agent at an unfamiliar repo to explain what it does and generate the docs that never existed. Plans are saved as editable Markdown you can iterate on and check in.

Model selection \& Auto:

Access frontier models tuned to run best in Cursor. Pick one per task, switch mid-agent, or let Auto route by cost, balance, or intelligence. Orgs can lock models per team.

Rules \& skills:

Rules always apply as guardrails; skills teach how a task should be done. Both are files you check into the repo, and can live at personal, project, or organization level.

Context, sub-agents \& Run Mode:

Track the context window and use /summarize to compress it. Give work its own sub-agent context, and use Run Mode to control approvals from auto-review to full YOLO.

segments.heading: Core Concepts and Architectural Foundations of Cursor 101 part 2
segments.text: In this session on Cursor 101 part 2, the focus centers on understanding the practical design patterns and developer workflows enabled by modern AI-assisted engineering. As development teams adopt agentic systems, the boundaries between manual code authorship and automated synthesis begin to blur. The speakers emphasize that establishing reliable context is paramount: providing the right repository structure, explicit project rules, and scoped documentation allows the underlying models to generate precise, syntactically correct implementations. By anchoring the discussion in real-world scenarios, the talk demonstrates how engineering productivity accelerates when tools operate directly within the IDE, reducing friction and eliminating disruptive context switching across disjointed external interfaces.

segments.heading: Technical Implementation, Tooling, and Workflow Patterns
segments.text: Diving deeper into operational mechanics, the presentation details how specific platform capabilities interact to execute complex programming tasks. Key components such as Cursor, Cursor Agent work in concert to maintain project state and navigate intricate dependency graphs. The session highlights the importance of deterministic tool calling, background agent execution, and structured feedback loops. Developers are guided through concrete demonstrations showing how natural language prompts are parsed into multi-file diffs, verified against local unit tests, and iteratively refined before final commit. This pattern ensures high reliability across both legacy refactoring and greenfield service development.

segments.heading: Evaluation, Best Practices, and Future Directions
segments.text: The concluding segment addresses best practices for scaling agent-driven development across larger teams. Speakers discuss token efficiency, model selection economics, and safety guardrails required when granting agents access to internal APIs and production repositories. Teams must establish clear evaluation benchmarks to verify that automated contributions maintain rigorous security and code quality standards. By combining automated linting, continuous integration checks, and human-in-the-loop review, organizations can safely harness autonomous agents to resolve routine maintenance tasks, documentation updates, and cross-repository migrations while preserving engineering velocity.

title: Cursor Rules, Skills, and MCPs
description:
In this workshop, we break down rules, skills, MCPs, and sub-agents , and when to use each , building a real feature in Adobe's open-source React Spectrum repo.

Key topics covered:

Rules vs skills:

Rules are persistent instructions the agent always respects; skills are specialized helpers invoked only when needed. Both live as files in the .cursor folder.

Creating rules:

Use /create rule or plain language to set team, personal, or org standards. Examples: require an accessible name on every interactive component, or print localhost on each UI change.

Creating skills:

Save reusable workers as Markdown files. Invoke them with a slash command or let the model pick them up, and nest parent and child skills for bigger tasks.

MCPs:

Think of MCPs as APIs for agents. Connect tools like Granola, Slack, or Atlassian via OAuth to pull notes, raise Jira tickets, and publish Confluence documentation without leaving Cursor.

Sub-agents:

Each sub-agent gets its own context window. Spawn up to 8 per agent, and 8 more each, to preserve context without compression , great for standardizing how tickets get implemented.

Marketplace \& plugins:

Publish and share rules, skills, MCPs, and sub-agents from the marketplace. A plugin bundles several together, like Atlassian's MCP plus its skills.

title: Cursor x BCG: The New Rules of AI Competition
description:
In this session, BCG's Matthew Kropp and Cursor's Maxime Prades explore why token strategy is becoming the new basis of competitive advantage.

Key topics covered:

Token-based competition:

As intelligence becomes abundant and cheap, advantage no longer comes from hoarding scarce talent. It comes from applying tokens to business problems more productively than competitors.

Growth, not cost-cutting:

Across 107 public companies, the top token-usage quintile grew 16.5% versus 5.1% for the lowest. Winners use AI for compounding innovation and elastic capacity, not just labor substitution.

Return on Intelligence:

Evaluate AI projects by output value divided by labor plus token cost. Fund anything above your hurdle rate instead of capping spend, and compare projects on the same metric.

Tokens like capital:

Move accountability out of IT and book token spend as capex, opex, or COGS where value is created. Budget caps kill adoption, and usage tends to follow a power law.

The Cursor Router:

Launched for Enterprise, the router classifies each prompt and routes across intelligence, balance, and cost modes. Intelligence mode runs about 60% cheaper than Fable at equivalent satisfaction.

Adoption is the bottleneck:

Fewer than 10% of enterprise engineers use agents today. The real work is change management: helping every team, not just engineering, feel the "magic moment."

title: Data agent kit: Your coding agent can now query your data
description: In this episode of Hands On, host Annie Wang and Google Cloud developer advocate Jeff discuss the Data Agent Kit, a Google-built unified source for data engineering, data analytics, and data science that provides skills, MCP tools, and IDE integrations for AI coding environments.

segments.heading: What the Data Agent Kit is and what it provides
segments.text: The Data Agent Kit is a Google-built unified source for data engineering, data analytics, and data science. It provides three primary components: agent skills (a library of data engineering, data science, and analytics best practices that steer agents in how to use Data Cloud), MCP tools (which securely connect to Cloud Data Cloud products including BigQuery, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, and Spanner), and IDE integrations (extensions available in any VS Code fork including Cloud Code, Codex, and Antigravity).

segments.heading: Setting up the Data Agent Kit extension in Antigravity IDE
segments.text: The Data Agent Kit is available as an extension in the VS Code extension marketplace. Once installed, it adds a Data Agent Kit icon in the sidebar and a setup and configuration pane. Configuration options include setting a Google Cloud project, region, and billing project, plus enabling specific APIs. One-click MCP server provisioning is available for BigQuery, Cloud SQL, Spanner, AlloyDB, and Knowledge Catalog.

segments.heading: One-click MCP server setup for BigQuery and Cloud SQL
segments.text: The extension provides one-click enablement of MCP servers for each supported database product. Regions configure the MCP servers. Once a BigQuery MCP server is enabled, the IDE extension surfaces a side panel that brings the entire Data Cloud estate into a single view: BigQuery tables can be browsed, conversational analytics can be used to query data in natural language, and data assets can be searched across using Knowledge Catalog.

segments.heading: Conversational analytics and Knowledge Catalog integration
segments.text: Within the IDE extension, users can use conversational analytics to query BigQuery data using natural language, without writing SQL. Knowledge Catalog integration allows searching across all data assets from within the same side panel. The demo shows querying Cloud SQL directly from the IDE after connecting via the MCP server configuration.

segments.heading: Agent skills for steering coding agents on data tasks
segments.text: Agent skills give AI coding agents context and best practices for working with Data Cloud. Instead of a coding agent generating arbitrary SQL or guessing table schemas, the skills steer it with domain knowledge about BigQuery, Cloud SQL, and related tools. This improves accuracy and reduces hallucinations when agents write queries or interact with data infrastructure.

segments.heading: Who benefits: data personas and software engineers
segments.text: For data professionals, the kit consolidates tools normally spread across many browser tabs into one view. For software engineers without deep data expertise, the agent skills and conversational interface allow analyzing and modifying data without needing to know SQL or the schema in depth. The demo explicitly notes the kit helps people who do not normally work with data day-to-day.

title: Implementing DeepMind innovation: Deep research API
description: Deep dive into Google DeepMind's Deep Research API available on Google AI Studio and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Explains how Gemini uses post-training for iterative multi-step web search, data synthesis, inline chart generation, and MCP data connectors. Features financial intelligence provider FactSet demonstrating automated research reporting on financial assets.

segments.heading: DeepMind innovation strategy: bringing research directly to APIs
segments.text: Google's vertical integration (custom silicon, foundation models, enterprise agent platforms) allows translating DeepMind research breakthroughs directly into commercial APIs. The Deep Research API exposes the autonomous research capabilities powering consumer Gemini directly to software developers, automating multi-hour manual research workflows into minutes.

segments.heading: How the Deep Research agent works: iterative search and post-training
segments.text: Unlike standard one-shot search grounding, Deep Research uses a specialized reasoning loop: (1) Decomposes complex queries into search sub-hypotheses, (2) Executes iterative Google searches, evaluating domain authority and factuality, (3) Pulls proprietary internal data via MCP servers, (4) Synthesizes long-form reports with strict source citations, and (5) Renders visual charts and infographics automatically.

segments.heading: Hands-on developer walkthrough and API parameters
segments.text: Philipp Schmid demonstrates integrating the Deep Research API via Google AI Studio and Python SDKs. Developers configure search depth, domain inclusion filters, MCP data connectors, and structured output formatting, enabling autonomous research agents to power internal enterprise knowledge bases.

segments.heading: Customer case study: FactSet automated financial research
segments.text: Patrick Starling from FactSet demonstrates integrating the Deep Research API into institutional financial workflows. FactSet combines its proprietary financial market data with Deep Research web intelligence to generate comprehensive equity research briefs, ESG risk assessments, and earnings call syntheses for financial analysts.

title: Defining the agentic AI era
description: Join Google’s AI leadership to discuss how the rapid acceleration of model capabilities is transforming productivity and access to information in a new era of proactive, agentic AI.

segments.heading: Gemini 3.5 Flash: purpose-built for agentic workflows and coding
segments.text: Koray Kavukcuoglu (CTO of Google DeepMind) explains the design focus of Gemini 3.5 Flash: advancing reasoning, multimodal comprehension, and long-horizon agentic task execution beyond Gemini 3.0. Internally at Google, researchers and engineers stress-tested models on real software engineering and long-horizon workflows. The operational insights directly informed architectural adjustments in training to resolve performance bottlenecks on extended multi-step reasoning tasks.

segments.heading: Full-stack AI infrastructure: 8th-generation TPUs and inference optimization
segments.text: Jeff Dean (Chief Scientist) highlights Google's vertical integration spanning custom silicon to deployed user interfaces. The 8th-generation TPU architecture introduces dedicated design separations optimizing training throughput versus high-speed inference serving. Dean emphasizes that high-speed inference fundamentally alters user experience: when agents execute tasks autonomously on a user's behalf, low latency compounds across dozens of iterative tool calls and subagent steps.

segments.heading: Rethinking search latency in an agentic paradigm
segments.text: Liz Reid (Head of Search) describes how latency expectations adapt to task complexity. For quick factual queries, users demand millisecond responses. For complex, multi-source synthesis or custom tool generation (such as building an interactive weekend planner), users comfortably tolerate a 30 to 60-second processing window. Search incorporates Gemini 3.5 Flash and Antigravity SDK components under the hood, routing multi-step queries across specialized backend databases (finance, sports, travel) through general reasoning rather than hardcoded query templates.

segments.heading: Gemini Spark: proactive 24/7 background agent workflows
segments.text: Josh Woodward (VP of Google Labs and Gemini App) outlines Gemini Spark, an always-on background agent. Key use cases include: automated morning information syntheses; conditional triggers (monitoring priority communications from executive leadership, conducting background research, and drafting responses without automatically sending); personalized sports updates delivered in a fan-tailored voice; and autonomous document/slide deck generation.

segments.heading: Amdahl's law and tool latency: the next performance bottleneck
segments.text: Jeff Dean notes that as inference speed and model compute times approach near-zero, external tool execution becomes the dominant system bottleneck under Amdahl's law. Tools designed for human interaction speeds (listing files, running heavy scripts, spinning up slow runtimes) severely limit autonomous agent throughput. Dean cites an internal example where Google engineers used Gemini to translate legacy internal tooling from slow Python implementations into optimized Go code in a single night, delivering 10x to 20x speedups in tool execution.

segments.heading: Machine-readable context: DESIGN.md and the elimination of PRDs
segments.text: Josh Woodward discusses how internal software engineering workflows have moved away from traditional product requirement documents (PRDs). Product teams increasingly write structured markdown context files (such as DESIGN.md, open-sourced via the Stitch project) that encode architectural boundaries, design tokens, and constraints in machine-consumable form, allowing agentic coding harnesses to implement UI and backend features directly.

segments.heading: Organizational transformation: the asynchronous engineering Renaissance
segments.text: Panelists describe how daily workflows have evolved across Google leadership. Executive and engineering roles now delegate substantive tasks asynchronously to background agents overnight or between meetings. Liz Reid emphasizes how AI tools dissolve traditional job boundaries: product managers can directly prototype and adjust UI stylesheets, and engineers can debug performance issues in unfamiliar legacy codebases by instructing agents to implement and benchmark alternative concurrency patterns.

segments.heading: Bespoke software generation: shifting from static apps to autonomous tools
segments.text: The panel highlights creative generation tools such as Google Flow, where filmmakers and artists vibe-code custom shaders, lighting pipelines, and UI tools directly within the creative suite. Jeff Dean observes that historical software engineering required standardizing rigid applications due to high development costs; agentic generation enables on-demand bespoke software tailored to specific users, tasks, or ephemeral queries.

title: A new era of discovery: AI and the frontiers of science with Demis Hassabis
description: We are at an incredibly exciting and consequential moment for AI. Join Google DeepMind co-founder and CEO Demis Hassabis for a conversation about how AI is helping to solve some of the most complex problems in science, and why we are on the cusp of a new golden age of discovery and exploration.

segments.heading: Foothills of the singularity: AGI timeline around 2030
segments.text: Demis Hassabis elaborates on his I/O keynote statement that we are standing in the foothills of the singularity. He defines singularity not in the specific Kurzweil sense but as a descriptor for the era that AGI precipitates: a moment so transformative that making predictions beyond it becomes unreliable because so much will change. He places AGI arrival at around 2030, plus or minus a year, based on current trajectory. He describes 2026-2027 as the period when people are starting to feel the acceleration, pointing to agentic systems as the leading indicator. His personal marker: he can now vibe-code a game prototype in a spare hour or two that would have taken six months before.

segments.heading: The Einstein test as the AGI threshold
segments.text: Hassabis clarifies that AGI will not arrive as a single dramatic moment but as a gradual, fast improvement. His personal test for full AGI is what he calls the Einstein test: imagine a frontier model with a knowledge cutoff of 1901. Could it independently derive the insights Einstein produced in his 1905 miracle year, including special relativity? Current systems clearly cannot. Hassabis sees no fundamental reason why future systems should not be able to, but this requires a kind of creative leap or genuine insight that current models lack. That creativity and leap-of-insight quality is what he is specifically watching for.

segments.heading: Google's competitive position: full-stack advantage
segments.text: Hassabis argues that Google's main structural advantage is its unique full-stack position: chips, data centers, cloud, frontier lab, and billion-user consumer products that already have AI embedded. No other organization has all of these simultaneously. The biggest recent change is rewriting the tech stack from the ground up to be AI-first and then agent-first, enabling direct deployment of the latest model improvements across all surfaces at massive scale. Consumer metrics cited: Gemini app at 900 million monthly active users with significant recent growth. AI Mode in Search is described as unbelievably popular. On small, efficient models: critical for serving billions of users internally and for enterprise customers at scale.

segments.heading: The AI backlash: why, and what to do about it
segments.text: Hassabis acknowledges the backlash but disagrees with how some peers communicate about AI. His framing: AI will be 10 times the impact of the Industrial Revolution, possibly 10 times faster (over a decade vs. a century), which he describes as roughly 100x the Industrial Revolution and possibly an underestimate. He does not claim certainty about net job effects: nobody knows whether there will be more or different jobs. His response to the backlash: demonstrate unequivocal concrete benefits, especially through AI for Science work in drug discovery, material science, mathematics, and energy. He is optimistic about human ingenuity to find productive uses, pointing to enthusiasm from young people at the India AI Summit who see AI democratizing access to tools that previously required teams of 50 experts.

segments.heading: AlphaFold: the decision to fold every protein and release it free
segments.text: A clip from the documentary The Thinking Game shows the moment in a DeepMind meeting when Hassabis realized the right deployment strategy for AlphaFold. The system was accurate and fast (folding a protein in seconds). Knowing approximately 200 million proteins were known to science, a back-of-envelope calculation told him the entire set could be folded with available compute. He instantly rejected the conventional approach (set up a server, have scientists submit sequences one by one) in favor of folding everything and releasing it free to the world. The database was built in partnership with the European Bioinformatics Institute in Cambridge and is accessible at essentially the speed of a Google Search. He frames this as the highest-impact deployment of the breakthrough possible.

segments.heading: Simulations, Genie, and weather prediction
segments.text: Hassabis has been interested in simulations since writing Theme Park in 1994, one of the first AI simulation games. He sees AI and simulations as complementary in two directions: AI can learn simulations of complex phenomena (WeatherNext learning to predict hurricane paths from data rather than solving Navier-Stokes equations by hand), and simulations can provide training data for AI systems. The Genie 3D interactive model is used to test Waymo self-driving systems in one-in-a-billion edge cases: what if there is a forest fire while driving, a biplane has made an emergency landing on the motorway, or an elephant appears in the road? These scenarios never appear in normal training data but reveal whether systems behave safely in extreme conditions.

segments.heading: What is missing from current AI systems: jagged intelligence and continual learning
segments.text:
Hassabis identifies two major gaps in current frontier models that AGI systems would not have:

1. Jagged intelligence: current models can excel at hard problems in certain framings but fail at strictly simpler versions of the same problem when presented slightly out of distribution. True general intelligence does not exhibit this inconsistency. A human expert who is good at a domain can solve easier problems in that domain too.

2. Continual learning: current models do not learn after deployment. Hassabis wants systems that can adapt and learn from experience after their initial training run, connected to personalization and the ability to update their knowledge to the user's specific context.

For I/O 2027, he expects agents embedded in real workflows as a major theme, and significant robotics advances from world models like Gemini robotics applied to multiple physical form factors.

segments.heading: Self-improvement and verifiable domains
segments.text: Hassabis identifies AI self-improvement as the central area of active investment across leading labs. Coding and mathematics are special because their outputs are verifiable: you can check whether a solution is correct. This verifiability enables generating synthetic training data and creates a compounding flywheel: better models write better code, which can be used to generate more training data, which trains better models. He describes this as evidence of a very interesting compounding dynamic. Cybersecurity becomes increasingly important as agents grow more powerful: ensuring that agents delegated to long-running tasks are doing exactly what they were instructed to do, no more and no less, in a verifiable and monitorable way.

segments.heading: Why Hassabis chose to build AI: the science motivation
segments.text:
Hassabis traces his motivation to childhood fascination with the biggest questions in science: the nature of reality, consciousness, time, quantum mechanics. He noticed that physics, his favorite subject, had not made fundamental progress since the early 20th century (Einstein, Heisenberg), and formed the hypothesis that brilliant human minds were approaching the limit of what they could comprehend unaided. Reading biographies of Feynman, Einstein, and Weinberg reinforced this. Combined with science fiction (Asimov's Foundation, Iain Banks's Culture series) and philosophy (Godel, Escher, Bach), he concluded that building AI was both the most interesting scientific artifact in itself and the most useful tool for advancing the other frontiers of knowledge. This motivation predates any external validation of the approach; he says he would still be working on AI even if it had remained a niche academic subject.

Sebastian Mallaby's biography The Infinity Machine is based on more than 30 hours of conversations in a London pub (coffee, not alcohol), which Hassabis says went fast because of the wide-ranging intellectual discussions.

segments.heading: Silicon Valley freneticism vs. the need for direction
segments.text: Hassabis observes that the Bay Area startup ecosystem has unmatched builder energy but also a freneticism that he cautions against. His specific concern: speed is favored over direction, but running at 100 miles per hour in the wrong direction is worse than standing still and thinking carefully about where to go. He argues that the next major advances will come from deep-tech applications of AI to hard science, which require years of sustained effort before results appear, and are incompatible with a purely high-velocity, reactive approach. His advice: build in quiet, reflective time to think deeply about what you are trying to accomplish and whether the direction is correct, not just whether you are moving fast.
